q: The claim is for vessels and land; he admits part of the vessels and denies the rest. What is the law?
options: He swears, and the oath extends to the land too
He is exempt: land is never sworn on
He swears only on the vessels
why: *Modeh be'miktzat* of the vessels obligates an oath, and it binds (*zokekin*) the land he denied.

q: He admits the land and denies the vessels. Must he swear?
options: No: an admission of land doesn't count toward *modeh be'miktzat*
Only if witnesses saw the vessels
why: Land is excluded from the oath of partial admission.

q: An unpaid bailee says of three cows: 'One was never given to me, one died by accident, one died by my negligence and I'll pay.' Is he a *modeh be'miktzat*?
options: Yes, and it isn't *heilakh*, since he isn't returning the cow
why: Rami bar Chama's baraita requires partial admission and partial denial from all four bailees.

q: According to the father of R. Aptoriki, do witnesses to part of a claim obligate an oath on the rest?
options: No: the oath comes only from the defendant's own admission
why: From "this is it": an oath on the admission of his own mouth, not on witnesses. R. Chiya, a tanna, disagrees.

q: What does R. Chiya learn from the second word of 'This is it' (*hu zeh*)?
options: The admission must be of the same kind as the claim (*mi'min ha'ta'anah*)
The oath must be in court
why: So one claimed wheat and admitted barley is exempt; Rabban Gamliel obligates him.

q: Witnesses saw a shepherd who denied receiving the animals eat two of them. Who swears, according to R. Zeira?
options: The owners swear and collect, since a proven robber can't swear
The shepherd swears on the rest
why: *She'kenegdo nishba ve'notel*. Abaye objected that the shepherd's own oath isn't credible.

q: Why doesn't Rav Nachman's *shevuat heset* lead to the owners swearing and collecting?
options: Both are rabbinic, and one rabbinic ordinance isn't built on another
Rav Nachman's oath is only for loans
why: The oath of inducement and 'the opposing party swears and collects' are both rabbinic ordinances.

q: Why isn't a hired shepherd presumed a robber, though an ordinary shepherd is?
options: A person sins for his own gain, and these animals aren't his
why: Rav Yehuda means one grazing his own animals; otherwise no one could hire a shepherd.

q: What exactly does each holder of the garment swear, according to Rav Huna?
options: 'I have a share in it, and not less than half'
why: "All is mine; but according to your statement": it keeps his claim and swears only to what the court grants.
